blocks.x: Core definitions
Permutation An ordered arrangement of objects, where the order in which objects are placed is important. E.g. the permutations of A, B, C are ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA.

Factorial notation, n!
For n ∈ ℕ, n! is defined as n! = n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)....1. Note that n! = n(n-1)!, 1! = 1 and 0! = 1.
Combination A selection of objects in which the order of selection does not matter — unlike a permutation.

Binomial coefficient
Written (n choose k), defined as n!/((n-k)!k!) — the same expression as ⁿCₖ — and used to build the terms of a binomial expansion.

c: Permutations, n taken k at a time

blocks.x: Permutation of Objects

A permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects, built and counted using factorial notation. This section also covers permutations with repeated objects, and the special case of circular permutations.
What is a permutation?

Permutation An ordered arrangement of objects is called a Permutation. For example, the possible permutations of the letters A, B, and C are: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA. In this case, order is very important.
The factorial notation
For n ∈ ℕ, n! ("n factorial") is a number defined as n! = n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)....1.
Note that n! = n(n-1)!, 1! = 1 and 0! = 1.
Permutations of n distinct objects

The number of permutations of n distinct/unlike objects, taken all together, is given by ⁿPₙ = n!/(n-n)! = n!.

The number of permutations of n distinct/unlike objects taken k at a time, where k < n, is given by ⁿPₖ = n!/(n-k)!.
Arranging the letters of PARK
Find the number of words (with or without meaning) that can be formed with the letters of the word PARK.

items: 1PARK has 4 distinct letters, all taken together — use ⁿPₙ = n!n = 4
2Compute 4! by multiplying down to 1.4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1

blocks.x: 4! = 24 words
Permutations with repeated objects

The number of permutations of n objects consisting of groups of which n₁ of the first group are alike, n₂ of the second group are alike, and so on for the kth group with nₖ objects which are alike is: n!/(n₁!n₂!...nₖ!), where n₁+n₂+n₃+...+nₖ = n.
If 8 students are to be accommodated in two 3-bed rooms and one 2-bed room, in how many ways can they be accommodated?

items: 1Identify the repeated groups: two rooms of 3 (alike within a room) and one room of 2.n₁ = 3, n₂ = 3, n₃ = 2, so n = n₁+n₂+n₃ = 3+3+2 = 8
2Apply the repeated-objects formula.n!/(n₁!n₂!n₃!) = 8!/(3!3!2!)
3Evaluate numerator and denominator separately.8! = 40320, 3!·3!·2! = 6·6·2 = 72
4Divide to get the final count.40320 ÷ 72 = 560

blocks.x: 560 ways
Circular permutations
Permutations that occur when objects are arranged in a circle are called circular permutations. The number of ways of arranging n different objects in a circle is given by n!/n = (n-1)!.
Permutations of 10 digits taken two at a time
The number of permutations of 10 distinct digits taken two at a time is:

items: 1Start from the general formula ⁿPₖ = n!/(n-k)! with n = 10, k = 2.¹⁰P₂ = 10!/(10-2)!
2Simplify the denominator.¹⁰P₂ = 10!/8!
3Expand 10! as 10.9.8! and cancel the common 8!.¹⁰P₂ = 10.9.8!/8!

blocks.x: ¹⁰P₂ = 90

blocks.x: Combination of Objects
A combination is a selection of objects in which order does not matter — the crucial contrast to a permutation. This section also links combinations back to permutations algebraically.
What is a combination?

Combination A combination is a selection of objects in which the order of selection does not matter. The number of ways in which k objects can be selected from n distinct objects, irrespective of their order, is defined by ⁿCₖ = n!/((n-k)!k!), or equivalently (n choose k) = n!/((n-k)!k!), where k < n.
Relationship between permutation and combination
ⁿCₖ = ⁿPₖ/k! or, equivalently, ⁿPₖ = k!·ⁿCₖ. A combination is simply a permutation with the k! internal re-orderings of the selected objects divided back out.
Selecting 4 students from a class of 20
In how many ways can 4 students be selected from a class of 20 to represent the class in an essay competition?

items: 1Order of selection doesn't matter, so use the combination formula with n = 20, k = 4.²⁰C₄ = 20!/(4!(20-4)!) = 20!/(4!16!)
2Expand 20! as 20.19.18.17.16! and cancel the common 16!.²⁰C₄ = 20.19.18.17.16!/4!16!
3Cancel 16!, leaving numerator over 4! = 4.3.2.1.²⁰C₄ = 20.19.18.17/4.3.2

blocks.x: ²⁰C₄ = 4845
Choosing a 2-player tennis team
Consider a team of 3 tennis players M, C, and J. A team consisting of 2 players is to be formed. In how many ways can we do so?

items: 1Since order does not matter in a combination, MC = CM, MJ = JM, and CJ = JC.Distinct teams: MC, MJ, CJ
2Apply the formula with n = 3, k = 2.³C₂ = 3!/((3-2)!2!) = 3!/(1!2!)

blocks.x: ³C₂ = 3 ways

blocks.x: The Binomial Theorem
The binomial theorem gives a formula for expanding (a+b)ⁿ using binomial coefficients. This section covers the theorem for a positive integer power, then generalises it to any rational index.
The binomial theorem (integer n)

The binomial theorem is a formula used to expand the binomial expression (a+b)ⁿ. Descriptions frequently use a shorthand notation for the coefficients of each term: numbers over each other enclosed in parenthesis, (n choose k) = n!/((n-k)!k!) — the binomial coefficient. For n > 0: (a+b)ⁿ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ (n choose k) aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ

blocks.x: The binomial theorem for any rational index

If n is any rational value, positive or negative, and -1 < x < 1, then the general binomial theorem is: (1+x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n-1)/2! x² + n(n-1)(n-2)/3! x³ + ... Remark: the first term of the binomial must be 1. To expand (a+x)ⁿ, it must first be written as aⁿ(1+x/a)ⁿ.
First three terms of (1 − x/2)¹⁰
Write down the first three terms in the expansion of (1 − x/2)¹⁰

items: 1Apply the general formula with n = 10, replacing x with (−x/2).(1+x)ⁿ = 1+nx+n(n-1)/2! x²+...
2Substitute n = 10 and (−x/2) into the first three terms.(1−x/2)¹⁰ = 1 + 10(−x/2) + [10(9)/2!](−x/2)² + ...
3Simplify each term: 10×(−x/2) = −5x; and 10×9/2 = 45, times (x²/4).= 1 − 5x + (45/4)x² + ...
